title: Naming the Trade-off
author: Ian Hallett
summary: This piece diagnoses why well-researched recommendations get picked apart in executive committees: presenting a single resolved option removes the part of the decision-making job senior leaders are actually there to do, forcing them to reconstruct the discarded alternatives through pointed questions that feel hostile but aren't. Drawing on a 2005 survey in which most CFOs admitted they would sacrifice long-term value to hit a short-term earnings target, and 2007 research showing strategic and business skill demands rise faster than interpersonal ones with seniority, the author argues senior audiences are specifically there to weigh trade-offs between competing, defensible options. His proposed method is to present exactly three options, each described in four elements — what it is, the trade-off it accepts, who else it affects, and what would have to be true for it to be correct — followed by a clear recommendation stating the trade-off accepted, why it's worth it, and when you'll know if you were wrong, illustrated with a concrete depot-closure example. A companion technique, the 'two-column test,' asks the presenter to rule two columns — this quarter and next year — for each option, since the quarter reliably wins when a decision-maker skips the second column, which is exactly what the 2005 CFO survey found happening at scale. The piece closes by insisting this method isn't about looking indecisive: a presenter still makes the recommendation, but showing three options is how they demonstrate their reasoning to people who need to see how they got there.

Argues bringing a single resolved recommendation removes the trade-off-weighing work senior leaders exist to do, making their follow-up questions feel hostile when they are really reconstructing discarded options.
Proposes a concrete three-option, four-line format (what it is, the trade-off accepted, who else is impacted, what would have to be true) illustrated with a depot-closure example.
Introduces a 'two-column test' — this quarter versus next year — as a five-minute way to surface the long-term costs a single-option recommendation tends to hide.
Ends with a practical exercise: write the sentence naming the trade-off, why it was worth accepting, and when you'd know if you were wrong, for a recommendation you've already sent.
quotes: In 2005, three finance academics, John Graham, Campbell Harvey and Shiva Rajgopal, surveyed more than four hundred chief financial officers and finance directors. A majority admitted they would sacrifice long-term value to hit a short-term earnings target.

That is why the questions can feel hostile. They are reconstructing the options you already discarded.

I recommend option B. The trade-off I am accepting is £2.3m of savings this year in exchange for keeping next-day coverage while we renegotiate two contracts. I think it is worth it because those two customers are fourteen per cent of revenue.
The left column is the easy one. The second is what the finance chiefs in the 2005 survey were skipping when they hit their earnings targets.
You still decide. The three options are how you show your working, and they let people senior to you see how you got there.
Write the sentence you would have put underneath it: the trade-off you accepted, why you judged it worth accepting, and when you would know if you were wrong.
